This chapter records the vocabulary in which the quantum Pauli basis test and its analysis are phrased: two-player one-round games and tensor product strategies, the consistency and state-dependent distance calculus for families of measurements, and conditionally linear functions and distributions, the class of question distributions used by the tests of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}. The presentation follows \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}; the distance calculus is imported there from \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP} and \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}.

\section{Measurements and observables}

\begin{definition}[POVMs, sub-measurements, and observables]\label{def:povm-conventions}
	\uses{def:submeasurement}
	% Finiteness of the outcome set is stated explicitly here; the source leaves it implicit,
	% and the measurement and submeasurement definitions referenced below assume finite
	% outcome sets.
	Quantum measurements are modeled as positive operator-valued measures (POVMs). A \emph{POVM} on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ is a family of positive semidefinite operators $\{M_a\}_{a \in S}$ indexed by outcomes $a$ ranging over a finite set $S$ such that $\sum_a M_a = \Id$; if the latter condition is relaxed to $\sum_a M_a \le \Id$, then $\{M_a\}$ is a \emph{sub-measurement}. (POVMs and sub-measurements are thus exactly the measurements and submeasurements of Definition~\ref{def:submeasurement}.) The probability that the measurement returns outcome $a$ on a state $\ket{\psi}$ is
	\[
		\Prb(a) = \bra{\psi} M_a \ket{\psi}\,.
	\]
	A POVM $M = \{M_a\}$ is \emph{projective} if each operator $M_a$ is a projector ($M_a^2 = M_a$); this automatically implies that $M_a M_b = M_b M_a = 0$ for distinct outcomes $a \ne b$. An \emph{observable} is a unitary matrix. A \emph{binary observable} is an observable $O$ such that $O^2 = \Id$, i.e.\ $O$ has eigenvalues in $\{-1,1\}$.

	Subscripts of a measurement index the outcome, and superscripts index different measurements. When the outcome of a measurement $\{M^x_{a,\,b}\}$ consists of two parts $a$ and $b$, we write $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$ for its \emph{marginals}
	\[
		M^x_a = \sum_b M^x_{a,\,b}\,, \qquad M^x_b = \sum_a M^x_{a,\,b}\,;
	\]
	for every $x$ both marginals are again POVMs.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Bracket notation for post-processed measurements]\label{def:bracket}
	\lean{MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement.postprocess}
	\leanok
	\uses{def:povm-conventions, def:post-processing}
	Let $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ be finite sets, let $\{M^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ be a family of POVMs indexed by $x \in \mathcal X$, and let $f \colon \mathcal A \to \mathcal B$ be an arbitrary function. We write $\bigl\{ M^x_{[f(\cdot)=b]} \bigr\}$ for the POVM derived from $\{M^x_a\}$ by applying the function $f$ to the outcome before returning it:
	\[
		M^x_{[f(\cdot)=b]} = \sum_{a\,:\,f(a)=b} M^x_a\,,
	\]
	and $M^x_{[f(\cdot)=b]} = 0$ when $b$ is not in the image of $f$. When the outcome $a$ has a natural interpretation as a tuple $(a_1,\dots,a_k)$, we also write, for $i \in \{1,\dots,k\}$,
	\[
		M^x_{[a_i=b]} = \sum_{(a_1,\dots,a_k)\,:\,a_i=b} M^x_{(a_1,\dots,a_k)}\,.
	\]
	For each fixed $x$ this is the post-processing operation of Definition~\ref{def:post-processing}.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[Naimark dilation for strategies]\label{rem:naimark-for-games}
	The symmetrization argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:symmetric-strat} below invokes Naimark dilation in the form of Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark} (stated and proved in Chapter~\ref{chap:projective}): a bipartite state together with two sub-measurement families can be replaced, without changing any of the correlations $\bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^y_b \ket{\psi}$, by a product-extended state together with projective sub-measurements on the enlarged spaces. When the input families are complete measurements, the dilated projective sub-measurements can be completed by assigning the residual projector of each family to one fixed outcome; the resulting projective measurements reproduce the same correlations on the extended state, since the correlation-preservation identity forces the extended state to lie in the range of the total projector of each dilated family. This completed form, with genuinely projective measurements, is the one used in Lemma~\ref{lem:symmetric-strat}; for the proof the source refers to Theorem 5.1 of \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}, which is stated for complete measurements. The source follows its statement of the dilation theorem with a sentence announcing an ``orthogonalization lemma'' from the literature that is never actually stated there; nothing in this chapter depends on it.
\end{remark}

\section{Games and strategies}
% Paper subsection label sec:strat kept for cross-reference fidelity.
\label{sec:strat}

\begin{definition}[Two-player one-round games]\label{def:game}
	A \emph{two-player one-round game} $\mathfrak G$ is specified by a tuple $(\mathcal X, \mathcal Y, \mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mu, D)$ where
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal Y$ are finite sets, called the \emph{question alphabets},
		\item $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$ are finite sets, called the \emph{answer alphabets},
		\item $\mu$ is a probability distribution over $\mathcal X \times \mathcal Y$, called the \emph{question distribution}, and
		\item $D \colon \mathcal X \times \mathcal Y \times \mathcal A \times \mathcal B \to \{0,1\}$ is a function, called the \emph{decision predicate}.
	\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Tensor product strategies]\label{def:tensor-product-strategy}
	\uses{def:game, def:povm-conventions}
	A \emph{tensor product strategy} $\mathcal S$ for a game $\mathfrak G = (\mathcal X, \mathcal Y, \mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mu, D)$ is a tuple $(\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ where
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $\ket{\psi}$ is a pure quantum state, i.e.\ a unit vector in $\mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ for finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces $\mathcal H_A$, $\mathcal H_B$,
		\item $A$ is a set $\{A^x\}$ such that for every $x \in \mathcal X$, $A^x = \{A^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ is a POVM on $\mathcal H_A$, and
		\item $B$ is a set $\{B^y\}$ such that for every $y \in \mathcal Y$, $B^y = \{B^y_b\}_{b \in \mathcal B}$ is a POVM on $\mathcal H_B$.
	\end{itemize}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Tensor product value]\label{def:tensor-product-value}
	\uses{def:tensor-product-strategy}
	The \emph{tensor product value} of a tensor product strategy $\mathcal S = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ with respect to a game $\mathfrak G = (\mathcal X, \mathcal Y, \mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mu, D)$ is
	\[
		\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S) = \sum_{x,\,y,\,a,\,b} \mu(x,y)\, D(x,y,a,b)\, \bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^y_b \ket{\psi}\,.
	\]
	For $v \in [0,1]$ we say that the strategy $\mathcal S$ \emph{passes (or wins) $\mathfrak G$ with probability $v$} if $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S) \ge v$. The \emph{tensor product value} of $\mathfrak G$ is
	\[
		\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G) = \sup_{\mathcal S} \operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S)\,,
	\]
	where the supremum is taken over all tensor product strategies $\mathcal S$ for $\mathfrak G$.
\end{definition}

Unless specified otherwise, all strategies considered in what follows are tensor product strategies, and we simply call them \emph{strategies}; similarly, we refer to $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G)$ as the \emph{value} of the game $\mathfrak G$.

% The source labels this definition def:projective-strategy. That label is already carried
% by the low individual degree test track (Chapter 2), where it names the strategy format
% specific to that test, so a distinct label is used here; see the following remark.
\begin{definition}[Projective strategies]\label{def:projective-strategy-general}
	\uses{def:tensor-product-strategy, def:povm-conventions}
	A strategy $\mathcal S = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ is \emph{projective} if all the measurements $\{A^x_a\}_a$ and $\{B^y_b\}_b$ are projective.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[Two uses of the term ``projective strategy'']\label{rem:projective-strategy-relation}
	Definition~\ref{def:projective-strategy-general} is the general notion: a strategy for an arbitrary nonlocal game all of whose measurements are projective. The low individual degree chapters use the same term for the concrete data of a two-prover strategy for the $(m,q,d)$ low individual degree test (Definition~\ref{def:projective-strategy} in Chapter~\ref{chap:test}); that definition is the specialization of the present notion to the question format of that particular test. The two usages occur in disjoint contexts.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Symmetric games and symmetric strategies]\label{def:symmetric-game}
	% Paper label: rem:symmetric-games (a definition environment carrying a rem: label in the
	% source); relabeled here to match the environment kind.
	\uses{def:game, def:tensor-product-strategy}
	A game $\mathfrak G = (\mathcal X, \mathcal Y, \mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mu, D)$ is \emph{symmetric} if the question and answer alphabets are the same for both players (i.e.\ $\mathcal X = \mathcal Y$ and $\mathcal A = \mathcal B$), the distribution $\mu$ is symmetric (i.e.\ $\mu(x,y) = \mu(y,x)$ for all $x,y$), and the decision predicate $D$ treats both players symmetrically (i.e.\ $D(x,y,a,b) = D(y,x,b,a)$ for all $x,y,a,b$).

	A strategy $\mathcal S = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ is \emph{symmetric} if $\ket{\psi}$ is a (pure) state in $\mathcal H \ot \mathcal H$, for some Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, that is invariant under permutation of the two factors, and the measurement operators of both players are identical.
\end{definition}

We often specify symmetric games $\mathfrak G$ and symmetric strategies $\mathcal S$ using a compact notation: we write $\mathfrak G = (\mathcal X, \mathcal A, \mu, D)$ and $\mathcal S = (\ket{\psi}, M)$, where $M$ denotes the set of measurement operators shared by both players.

% Source statement (references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:94-99) kept in
% its original form. The proof below records the approximate form the source argument
% establishes and leaves the final attainment step unproved; see rem:symmetric-strat-limit.
\begin{lemma}[Symmetrization of strategies for symmetric games]\label{lem:symmetric-strat}
	\uses{def:symmetric-game, def:tensor-product-value, def:projective-strategy-general}
	Let $\mathfrak G = (\mathcal X, \mathcal A, \mu, D)$ be a symmetric game such that $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G) = 1-\eps$ for some $\eps \ge 0$. Then there exists a symmetric and projective strategy $\mathcal S = (\ket{\psi}, M)$ such that $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S) \ge 1-\eps$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
	\uses{thm:naimark}
	The symmetrization argument establishes the following approximate form of the conclusion: for every $\eps' > \eps$ there exists a symmetric and projective strategy of value at least $1-\eps'$. Indeed, fix $\eps' > \eps$. Since $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G)$ is the supremum of the values of all strategies, there exists a strategy $\mathcal S' = (\ket{\psi'}, A, B)$ with $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S') \ge 1-\eps'$. Using Naimark dilation (Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark}), each dilated sub-measurement being completed to a projective measurement by assigning to one fixed outcome the residual projector of its family --- which changes no correlation on the extended state, as described in Remark~\ref{rem:naimark-for-games} above --- we may assume without loss of generality that $\ket{\psi'} \in \C^d_{A'} \ot \C^d_{B'}$ for some integer $d$ and that every $A^x$ and $B^x$ is a projective measurement. Let
	\[
		\ket{\psi} = \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}\, \bigl( \ket{0}_{A}\ket{1}_{B}\ket{\psi'}_{A'B'} + \ket{1}_{A}\ket{0}_{B}\ket{\psi'_\tau}_{A'B'} \bigr) \in \bigl(\C^2_{A} \ot \C^d_{A'}\bigr) \ot \bigl(\C^2_{B} \ot \C^d_{B'}\bigr)\,,
	\]
	where $\ket{\psi'_\tau}$ is obtained from $\ket{\psi'}$ by permuting the two players' registers; then $\ket{\psi}$ is invariant under permutation of the register pairs $AA'$ and $BB'$. For each question $x \in \mathcal X$ define the projective measurement $M^x = \{M^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ on $\C^2 \ot \C^d$ by
	\[
		M^x_a = \ket{0}\bra{0} \ot A^x_a + \ket{1}\bra{1} \ot B^x_a\,,
	\]
	and let each player measure $M$ on their pair of registers. Because the decision predicate $D$ of the symmetric game treats the two players symmetrically, the resulting symmetric projective strategy $\mathcal S = (\ket{\psi}, M)$ satisfies $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S) = \operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G, \mathcal S') \ge 1-\eps'$. Note that this construction preserves the value of the strategy it is applied to exactly.

	The statement asserts more, namely a single symmetric projective strategy of value at least $1-\eps$ itself. Passing from the family of strategies constructed above to one attaining the bound $1-\eps$ is an attainment step which the argument does not supply: the supremum defining $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G)$ in Definition~\ref{def:tensor-product-value} ranges over strategies of unbounded dimension and need not be attained. This step remains unproved; the obstruction, and the forms of the lemma that the argument does prove, are documented in \cite{gap:qpbt_symmetrization-attainment}. See also Remark~\ref{rem:symmetric-strat-limit}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Attainment in the symmetrization lemma]\label{rem:symmetric-strat-limit}
	The proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:symmetric-strat} yields, for each $\eps' > \eps$, a symmetric projective strategy of value at least $1-\eps'$. The conclusion as stated, at $\eps' = \eps$, does not follow from this: the dilated dimension $d$ may grow as $\eps' \downarrow \eps$, and the supremum defining $\operatorname{val}^*(\mathfrak G)$ in Definition~\ref{def:tensor-product-value} need not be attained by any strategy. The symmetrization construction itself is value-preserving, so the conclusion does hold whenever the hypothesis supplies an actual strategy of value at least $1-\eps$ rather than only the value of the game; every use of the lemma in the source proceeds from such a strategy, or from a strict lower bound on the value, and therefore consumes only what the proof establishes. The gap and the available repairs are documented in \cite{gap:qpbt_symmetrization-attainment}.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Commuting strategies]\label{def:comm-strategy}
	\uses{def:game, def:tensor-product-strategy}
	Let $\mathfrak G = (\mathcal X, \mathcal Y, \mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mu, D)$ be a game, and let $\mathcal S = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ be a strategy for $\mathfrak G$ such that $\mathcal H_A = \mathcal H_B$. We say that $\mathcal S$ is a \emph{commuting strategy for $\mathfrak G$} if for all question pairs $(x,y)$ in the support of $\mu$ (i.e.\ all $(x,y)$ with $\mu(x,y) > 0$) we have
	\[
		[A^x_a, B^y_b] = 0 \qquad \text{for all } a \in \mathcal A,\ b \in \mathcal B\,,
	\]
	where $[A,B] = AB - BA$ denotes the commutator.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Consistent measurements]\label{def:consistent-measurement}
	\uses{def:povm-conventions}
	Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite set, let $\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal H \ot \mathcal H$ be a state, and let $\{M_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ be a projective measurement on $\mathcal H$. We say that \emph{$\{M_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$} if and only if
	\[
		\forall a \in \mathcal A\,, \qquad M_a \ot \Id_B\, \ket{\psi} = \Id_A \ot M_a\, \ket{\psi}\,.
	\]
	When the state $\ket{\psi}$ is clear from context we simply say that $\{M_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ is consistent.
\end{definition}

The terminology arises from the fact that when the measurement $\{M_a\}$ is performed on both registers of $\ket{\psi}$, the probability of obtaining twice the same outcome is
\[
	\sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \ot M_a \ket{\psi} = \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Id_A \ot (M_a)^2 \ket{\psi} = \sum_a \bra{\psi} \Id_A \ot M_a \ket{\psi} = 1\,,
\]
where the first equality is by the definition of consistency, the second uses that $\{M_a\}$ is projective, and the last uses $\sum_a M_a = \Id$.

\begin{definition}[Consistent strategies]\label{def:consistent-strategy}
	\uses{def:consistent-measurement, def:projective-strategy-general}
	Let $\mathcal S = (\ket{\psi}, A, B)$ be a projective strategy with state $\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal H \ot \mathcal H$, for some Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, defined on question alphabets $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal Y$ and answer alphabets $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal B$, respectively. We say that $\mathcal S$ is \emph{consistent} if for all $x \in \mathcal X$ the measurement $\{A^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$, and for all $y \in \mathcal Y$ the measurement $\{B^y_b\}_{b \in \mathcal B}$ is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$.
\end{definition}

We almost always restrict attention to symmetric strategies; in this case consistency implies that whenever both players are sent the same question, they provide the same answer.

\begin{definition}[PCC and SPCC strategies]\label{def:spcc}
	\uses{def:projective-strategy-general, def:consistent-strategy, def:comm-strategy, def:symmetric-game}
	We say that a strategy $\mathcal S$ for a game $\mathfrak G$ is \emph{PCC} if it is projective, consistent, and commuting for $\mathfrak G$. Additionally, we say that a PCC strategy $\mathcal S$ is \emph{SPCC} if it is furthermore symmetric.
\end{definition}

\section{Distance measures}

\begin{definition}[Distance between states]\label{def:state-distance}
	Let $\{\ket{\psi_n}\}_{n \in \N}$ and $\{\ket{\psi'_n}\}_{n \in \N}$ be two families of states in the same space $\mathcal H$. For a function $\delta \colon \N \to [0,1]$ we say that $\{\ket{\psi_n}\}$ and $\{\ket{\psi'_n}\}$ are \emph{$\delta$-close}, denoted $\ket{\psi} \approx_\delta \ket{\psi'}$, if
	\[
		\lVert \ket{\psi_n} - \ket{\psi'_n} \rVert^2 = O(\delta(n))\,.
	\]
	The dependence of the states and of $\delta$ on the indexing parameter $n$ is generally left implicit; we write, e.g., $\ket{\psi}$ for $\ket{\psi_n}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Consistency between POVMs]\label{def:consistency}
	\uses{def:povm-conventions, def:state-distance}
	Let $\mathcal X$ be a finite set and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mathcal X$. Let $\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ be a quantum state, and for all $x \in \mathcal X$ let $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ be POVMs. We write
	\[
		A^x_a \ot \Id_B \simeq_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a
	\]
	on state $\ket{\psi}$ and distribution $\mu$ if
	\[
		\E_{x \sim \mu} \sum_{a \ne b} \bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^x_b \ket{\psi} = O(\delta)\,.
	\]
	In this case we say that $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ are \emph{$\delta$-consistent} on $\ket{\psi}$. As in Definition~\ref{def:state-distance}, the $O(\cdot)$ refers to families of POVMs and states indexed by an implicit parameter $n \in \N$, and is taken as $n \to \infty$.
\end{definition}

A measurement that is consistent on $\ket{\psi}$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:consistent-measurement} is $0$-consistent with itself on the same state under the singleton distribution, and vice versa: if $\sum_a \bra{\psi} M_a \ot M_a \ket{\psi} = 1$, then $M_a \ot \Id\, \ket{\psi} = \Id \ot M_a\, \ket{\psi}$ for every $a$, by the equality case of the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality applied outcome by outcome.

% (references/neexp-paper/05_quantum_preliminaries.tex:385-391), from which the distance
% calculus is imported; the POVM case is singled out after the display.
\begin{definition}[State-dependent distance between operator families]\label{def:povm-distance}
	\uses{def:povm-conventions, def:state-distance}
	Let $\mathcal X$ and $\mathcal A$ be finite sets and $\mu$ a distribution on $\mathcal X$. Let $\ket{\psi} \in \mathcal H$ be a quantum state, and for all $x \in \mathcal X$ let $\{M^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ and $\{N^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal A}$ be two families of linear operators on $\mathcal H$. We say that \emph{$\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ are $\delta$-close on state $\ket{\psi}$ and under distribution $\mu$} if
	\[
		\E_{x \sim \mu} \sum_a \lVert (M^x_a - N^x_a)\, \ket{\psi} \rVert^2 \le O(\delta)\,,
	\]
	and we write $M^x_a \approx_\delta N^x_a$ to denote this when the state $\ket{\psi}$ and the distribution $\mu$ are clear from context. This distance is referred to as the \emph{state-dependent} distance. The principal case is that in which $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{N^x_a\}$ are POVMs on $\mathcal H$, and we then speak of the state-dependent distance between the POVMs; but the relation is used for arbitrary operator families --- for instance for products of measurement operators, or for commutators compared against the identically zero family, as in Lemma~\ref{lem:commutation-analysis} below.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Distance between strategies]\label{def:strategy-distance}
	\uses{def:tensor-product-strategy, def:state-distance, def:povm-distance}
	Let $\mathfrak G = (\mathcal X, \mathcal Y, \mathcal A, \mathcal B, \mu, D)$ be a nonlocal game and let $\mathcal S = (\psi, A, B)$ and $\mathcal S' = (\psi', A', B')$ be strategies for $\mathfrak G$. For $\delta \in [0,1]$ we say that \emph{$\mathcal S$ is $\delta$-close to $\mathcal S'$} if the following conditions hold.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item The states $\ket{\psi}, \ket{\psi'}$ are states in the same Hilbert space $\mathcal H_A \ot \mathcal H_B$ and are $\delta$-close.
		\item For all $x \in \mathcal X$ and $y \in \mathcal Y$, we have $A^x_a \approx_\delta (A')^x_a$ and $B^y_b \approx_\delta (B')^y_b$, with the approximations holding under the distribution $\mu$ (i.e.\ under its corresponding marginals), on either $\ket{\psi}$ or $\ket{\psi'}$.
	\end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}[Asymptotic reading of the distance relations]\label{rem:asymptotic-distance}
	Definitions~\ref{def:state-distance}, \ref{def:consistency}, and \ref{def:povm-distance} are asymptotic: every $\approx_\delta$ and $\simeq_\delta$ statement refers to families of states and measurement families indexed by an implicit parameter $n \in \N$, and the $O(\cdot)$ is taken as $n \to \infty$. None of these relations is a pointwise inequality with an explicit constant. By contrast, the corresponding relations used in the low individual degree chapters (Definitions~\ref{def:simeq} and~\ref{def:approx_delta}) carry no hidden constant. Any explicit quantitative version of the present relations therefore retains the constants absorbed into the $O(\cdot)$; for instance, the triangle inequality of Lemma~\ref{fact:triangle} carries a factor $2$ inside the $O(\cdot)$.
\end{remark}

We record several useful facts about the consistency measure and the state-dependent distance. For the statements imported without proof, readers are referred to Sections~4.4 and~4.5 of \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}.

\begin{lemma}[Consistency versus closeness; Facts 4.13 and 4.14 in \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}]\label{fact:agreement}
	\uses{def:consistency, def:povm-distance}
	For POVMs $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$, the following hold.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item If $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \simeq_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a$, then $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \approx_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a$.
		\item If $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \approx_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a$ \emph{and} $\{A^x_a\}$ and $\{B^x_a\}$ are projective measurements, then $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \simeq_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a$.
		\item If $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \approx_\delta \Id_A \ot B^x_a$ and either $\{A^x_a\}$ or $\{B^x_a\}$ is a projective measurement, then $A^x_a \ot \Id_B \simeq_{\delta^{1/2}} \Id_A \ot B^x_a$.
	\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
	Stated in the source without proof; these are Facts 4.13 and 4.14 of \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. For the first item, expand each term $\lVert (A^x_a \ot \Id - \Id \ot B^x_a)\ket{\psi} \rVert^2$ and use $ (A^x_a)^2 \le A^x_a$, $(B^x_a)^2 \le B^x_a$ together with completeness of the two POVMs: summing over $a$ and averaging over $x$ bounds the total by at most twice the off-diagonal mass, which is $O(\delta)$ by hypothesis. When both families are projective the two operator inequalities hold with equality, so the expansion equals exactly twice the off-diagonal mass; reading this identity in the other direction gives the second item. For the third item, write the off-diagonal mass $\sum_{a \ne b} \bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^x_b \ket{\psi}$ as an inner product involving $(A^x_a \ot \Id - \Id \ot B^x_a)\ket{\psi}$, using projectivity of one of the two families, and apply the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality; this route costs a square root in the error.
\end{proof}

```lean
/-- Soundness function of the Pauli basis test; argument order (ε, m, d, q)
everywhere, per rem:delta-qld-argument-order. Real rpow throughout. -/
noncomputable def deltaQld (a b ε : ℝ) (m d q : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  a * ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ) ^ a *
    (ε ^ b + (q : ℝ) ^ (-b) + (2 : ℝ) ^ (-(b * ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ))))

/-- thm:pauli (qpbt-paper 08_…tex:1426-1447): soundness of the Pauli basis test. -/
theorem pauli_soundness :
    ∃ a b : ℝ, 1 ≤ a ∧ 0 < b ∧ b < 1 ∧
      ∀ (P : AdmissibleParams) [FieldModel P.q] (ε : ℝ), 0 < ε →
        ∀ S : Strategy (pauliBasisTest P), 1 - ε ≤ S.value →
          ∃ (ιA' ιB' : Type) (_ : Fintype ιA') (_ : DecidableEq ιA')
            (_ : Fintype ιB') (_ : DecidableEq ιB')
            (φA : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιA →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
                    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × PauliRegister P))
            (φB : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιB →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
                    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιB' × PauliRegister P))
            (aux : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × ιB')), ‖aux‖ = 1 ∧
            -- item 1: ‖φA ⊗ φB ψ − aux ⊗ EPR_q^{⊗M}‖ ≤ δ_qld  (squared distance,
            -- via stateDistSq and deltaQld²; or state with ‖·‖ directly — either
            -- form is acceptable, document the choice)
            ‖isometryTensor φA φB S.ψ - idealState P aux‖
                ≤ deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q ∧
            -- item 2, for both players and both bases, summation over u ∈ F_q^M,
            -- w.r.t. the ideal state; O(·) constants absorbed into a (see (e)8)
            ∀ W : PauliKind,
              (∑ u : PauliRegister P,
                ‖(heteroKron
                    (conjIsometry φA ((S.A (pauliQuestion P W)).effect
                      (PauliAnswer.pauliOutcome u) ...decoded))
                    (1 : Op (ιB' × PauliRegister P))
                  - pauliProjOnA'' P W u).mulVec (idealState P aux)‖ ^ 2)
                ≤ deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q ∧
              (symmetric B-side bound)
```

Supporting definitions in Soundness.lean (all NEW, Lean-only):
`idealState P aux := reindexState prodShuffle (vecTensor aux (eprState (PauliRegister P)))`;
`pauliQuestion P W : (pauliBasisTest P).QuestionA := (PauliType.pauli W, 0)` (the
`(Pauli, W)` question has content `0`, image of the 0-level CL function);
`pauliProjOnA'' P W u : Op ((ιA' × Reg) × (ιB' × Reg))` places `pauliProj W u` on the
`A''` factor, identity elsewhere (and the `B''` analogue). The A-side measurement
outcome family is the sub-family of `S.A` at outcomes `PauliAnswer.pauliOutcome u`
(other constructors carry no mass in the ideal comparison; define the family by
pattern-matching `PauliAnswer → Op` with `0` on the other constructors — this is the
faithful reading of "answer summation over `u ∈ F_q^M`").

## (e) Settled encoding decisions (do not re-derive)

1. **Polynomials — representative convention** (issue #0004, `def:polynomials-degree`):
   polynomial-valued objects are representatives, not function classes. Reuse
   `MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.polyFunc` where a polynomial *class* is quantified.
   Game *answers* are finite coefficient tuples exactly as printed in the paper
   ("given by its d+1 coefficients"): `Fin (d+1) → K`, resp. `Fin (m*d+1) → K`.
   Do not reuse `LDT.AxisLinePolynomial`/`DiagonalLineAnswer` (the LDT diagonal answer
   is function-encoded and `Parameters`-bundled; a bridge can come later).
   `def:ld-meas`/`PolyMeas` are NOT in this closure — do not build them now.
2. **Distributions — match LDT, not PMF**: the LDT question distributions use
   `MIPStarRE.LDT.Distribution` (Finset-supported, real weights, `Error := ℝ`) with
   `IsProbability`, `avgOver`, `map`, `uniformDistribution`, `uniformOnFinset`

   `DistributionPMF` bridge, never in game-facing statements.

   (`Quantum/Measurement.lean`) as the POVM carrier; marginals and the bracket
   notation are `Measurement.postprocess` (already `\leanok` for ch12 `def:bracket`).

4. **States**: pure states as unit vectors of `EuclideanSpace ℂ ι` (the theorem's
   conclusion needs vector norms, isometries `→ₗᵢ[ℂ]` — reuse
   `Quantum/FiniteHilbert.lean` patterns — and `eprState`). The density-matrix
   `LDT.QuantumState` layer is NOT used in the QPBT games layer.
5. **Field model**: reuse `MIPStarRE.LDT.FieldModel q` (bundled `K ≃ Fin q`). The χ
   map (eq:chi-func) interprets `s : K` as an integer through `FieldModel.equiv`;
   the finite-field trace is the basis-independent `Algebra.trace (ZMod 2) K`
   (= Tr of `Algebra.leftMulMatrix`, i.e. eq:def-trace). The self-dual normal basis
   and `def:binary-representation` are NOT in the statement closure and are deferred
   (see OPEN-6). `canonicalComplement` is defined basis-freely by the pivot
   characterization — `j` is a pivot of `W` iff restricting to coordinates `≤ j`
   increases rank — which agrees with the source's RREF construction by the
   basis-independence noted in `def:canonical-complement` (equivalence proof deferred).
6. **Qudit indexing**: the `M = 2^m` qudits and the vectors `F_q^M` are indexed by
   `Cube m := Fin m → Bool`. Never introduce `Fin (2^m)`; `M` appears only as
   `Fintype.card (Cube m)` in docstrings.
7. **Prose claims inside blueprint definitions become companion lemmas**: CL-level
   assertions ("`L_ALine` is a 2-level CL function"), uniformity of `χ(s)`,
   well-definedness remarks — each a named `sorry` lemma next to the definition, not
   a definitional obligation. Definitions themselves are direct and computable-shaped.
8. **Asymptotic `≈`/O(·) → quantitative functionals**: `def:state-distance` /
   `def:povm-distance` are encoded as explicit real error quantities (`stateDistSq`,
   `opFamilyDistSq`), mirroring how the LDT track already quantifies `≃`/`≈`
   (cf. rem:asymptotic-distance). The implicit universal constants of the blueprint's
   `≈_δ` are absorbed into the existentially quantified constant `a` of
   `pauli_soundness`; record this in the theorem docstring.
9. **Win predicates are `Bool`-valued**, answer alphabets are sum types, and
   "answers not of the prescribed form are rejected" is a predicate clause (match on
   constructor shape). Question alphabets are `Type × ambient-space` pairs — contents
   are full ambient vectors `ι → K` (images of the CL maps), not per-type refined

    prefactor `a(md)^a` — per rem:delta-qld-argument-order; do not copy the classical

   880	\subsection{The Pauli basis test}
   881	\label{sec:pauli-verifier}
   882	
   883	We introduce the quantum low-degree test of~\cite{natarajan2018low} in the form
   884	of a slight modification to it by~\cite{NW19} known as the \emph{Pauli basis
   885	  test}.
   886	Informally, the quantum low-degree test asks the players to measure a large
   887	number of qubits and return a highly compressed version of the measurement
   888	outcome.
   889	The Pauli basis test simply asks that the players return their uncompressed
   890	measurement outcomes, and it is designed by direct reduction to the quantum
   891	low-degree test.
   892	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-game} we describe the Pauli basis test as a nonlocal
   893	game $\game^\pauli$ and show that its question distribution is implementable via
   894	a CL distribution, as we did with the classical low-degree test in
   895	Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   896	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-complexity} we exhibit canonical parameters for the
   897	Pauli basis test and give bounds on the time complexity of executing the test.
   898	
   899	\subsubsection{The game}
   900	\label{sec:qld-game}
   901	
   902	We start by discussing parameter settings.
   903	The game $\game^\pauli$ is parametrized by a tuple
   904	\[\qldparams = (q,m,d)\;,\] where $q,m,d \in \N$ are integers. 
   905	We sometimes write $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
   906	Pauli basis test on the parameters.
   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,
   931	receives outcome $h_X$, and outputs $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$.
   932	For technical reasons that will become clear shortly,
   933	it will be convenient for the prover's measurement to have two outcomes rather than~$q$ outcomes.
   934	To accomplish this, the verifier also provides the prover with an element $r_X \in \F_q$;
   935	given this, the prover should output not $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$ but $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$, which is an element of $\F_2$.
   936	Similarly, on the $Z$ side, suppose the prover is provided $r_Z \in \F_q$,
   937	performs $\{\tau_h^Z\}$ to receive $h_Z$, and outputs $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \in \F_2$.
   938	Together, these two are a pair of two-outcome measurements, one in the~$X$ basis and one in the~$Z$ basis,
   939	and as it turns out, this pair of measurements either commutes with each other or anticommutes with each other
   940	(this is why we modified the measurements to have only two outcomes).
   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}
   946	If $\gamma = 0$, then these two measurements commute, and if $\gamma = 1$, then these two measurements anticommute
   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).
   948	In the $\gamma = 0$ case, the verifier can check whether these two measurements commute by performing the ``commutation check'',
   949	which asks the provers to simultaneously measure both $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$ and $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z)$ and report their values.
   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.
   957	
   958	\begin{definition}[Admissible parameters]\label{def:admissible}
   959	  We say that the tuple $\qldparams=(q, m, d)$ is \emph{admissible} if $q$ is
   960	  an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $m | q$.
   961	\end{definition}

   964	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   965	We now describe the question distribution of the game $\game^\pauli$, and show
   966	that it is a (typed) CL distribution.
   967	The question types in the game $\game^\pauli$ are
   968	\begin{equation}
   969	  \label{eq:pauli-type}
   970	  \type^\pauli= \bigl( \{\Point, \ALine, \DLine, \Pauli, \Pair \} \times \{X,Z\} \bigr)
   971	  \cup \type^\ms \cup \{\Pair\}\;,
   972	\end{equation}
   973	where $\type^\ms$ is the question type set of the Magic Square game defined in
   974	Section~\ref{sec:ms}.
   975

   978	
   979	Before presenting the CL functions of the Pauli basis test, we first give an
   980	intuitive description of the question distribution of the Pauli basis test: a
   981	pair of questions $((\tvar_\alice, x_\alice), (\tvar_\bob, x_\bob))$ in
   982	$\game^\pauli$ can be sampled via the following procedure:
   983	
   984	\begin{enumerate}
   985	\item Sample a pair of types by sampling an edge $(\tvar_\alice, \tvar_\bob)$ of
   986	  the graph $G^\pauli$ given in Figure~\ref{fig:type-graph-pauli} uniformly at
   987	  random (including the self-loops).
   988	\item Sample the following uniformly at random:
   989		\begin{enumerate}
   990		\item (\emph{Points}) $u_\xpt,u_\zpt \in \F_q^m$,
   991		\item (\emph{Directions}) $s \in \F_q$, $v \in \F_q^m$,
   992	  \item (\emph{Qubit basis for (anti-)commutation}) $r_\xpt,r_\zpt \in \F_q$.
   993		\end{enumerate}
   994	\item For $w \in \AB$ and $W\in\{X,Z\}$,
   995		\begin{enumerate}
   996	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Point, W)$, then set $x_w = u_W$,
   997	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\ALine, W)$, then set $x_w = (u_0,s)$, where $u_0 =
   998	    L^\lnf_{e_i}(u_W)$, with $i = \chi(s)$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-game} for
   999	    definition of $L^\lnf$ and $\chi(s)$),
  1000	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\DLine,W)$, then set $x_w = (u_0,s,v')$, where $i =
  1001	    \chi(s)$, $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v)$, and $u_0 = L^\lnf_{v'}(u_W)$,
  1002	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Constraint_i$ for some $i\in\{1,\ldots,6\}$, then set
  1003	    $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1004	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Variable_j$ for some $j\in\{1,\ldots,9\}$, then set $x_w
  1005	    = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1006	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Pair$, then set $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1007	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Pair, W)$, then set $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1008	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Pauli, W)$, then set $x_w = 0$.

    48	\label{sec:qld-prelim}

    51	\begin{definition}
    52	Given integer $d,m$ and a prime power $q$ we denote by $\ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$ the set of polynomials in $m$ variables
    53	  with \emph{individual} degree at most $d$ in each variable. When the field is clear from context we write $\ideg_{d,m}$. 	
    54		When
    55	  the number of variables is clear from context we
    56	  write $\ideg_d$. We denote by $\deg_{d}$ the set of polynomials with
    57	  \emph{total} degree at most $d$.
    58	\end{definition}
    59	
    60	Recall the low-degree code defined in \Cref{sec:ld-encoding}, in which vectors $h \in \F_q^\nqubits$ get mapped to polynomials $g_h \in \ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$ such that for every $u \in \{0,1\}^m$, $g_h(u) = h_u$ where the coordinates of $h$ are indexed by binary strings of length $m$. For $x\in \F_q^m$, recall the definition of the vector $\ind_m(x) \in \F_q^\nqubits$ from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}. Recall also the finite field trace $\tr(\cdot)=\tr_{q\to 2}(\cdot):\F_q\to\F_2$, where $q=2^k$ for odd $k$, defined in Section~\ref{sec:subfields}. 
    61	
    62	
    63	
    64	Call a tuple $\omega = (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,r_\xpt,r_\zpt) \in (\F_q^m)^2
    65	\times (\F_q)^2$ \emph{anticommuting} if the quantity 
    66	 \[\gamma\,=\,\tr ((r_\xpt \cdot
    67	\ind_m(u_\xpt)) \cdot (r_\zpt \cdot \ind_m(u_\zpt)))\]
    68	introduced in~\Cref{eq:gamma-value} is not $0$, and \emph{commuting} if $\gamma=0$.
    69	
    70	\begin{fact}
    71	\label{fact:omega-anticomm-prob}
    72		The probability that a tuple $\omega= (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$ sampled uniformly at random from $(\F_q^m)^2 \times (\F_q)^2$
    73		is anti-commuting is at least 
    74		\[
    75			(1 - q^{-m}) \cdot (1 - q^{-1}) \cdot \Big (1 - \frac{md}{q} \Big )  \cdot \frac{1}{2} \geq \Big (1 - \frac{3md}{q} \Big ) \cdot \frac{1}{2}.
    76		\]
    77		The probability that $\omega$ is commuting is also at least $\Big(1 - \frac{3md}{q} \Big ) \cdot \frac{1}{2}$.
    78	\end{fact}
    79	\begin{proof}
    80		First, note that $\ind_m(u_\xpt) = 0$ if and only if $u_\xpt = 0$. If $u_\xpt=0$ then $\omega$ is commuting. Otherwise, if $u_\xpt \neq 0$, then observe that for all $r_\xpt, r_\zpt, u_\zpt$,
    81		\begin{align*}
    82			\tr( (r_\xpt \cdot \ind_m(u_\xpt)) \cdot (r_\zpt \cdot
    83	                \ind_m(u_\zpt))) &= \tr( r_\xpt r_\zpt (\ind_m(u_\xpt) \cdot \ind_m(u_\zpt))) \\
    84									&= \tr( (r_\xpt r_\zpt) \cdot g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt))\;,
    85		\end{align*}
    86		where $g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}$ is a nonzero polynomial in $\ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$.
    87		
    88		If $r_\xpt = 0$, then $\omega$ is commuting. Condition on $r_\xpt \neq 0$.  Since $g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}\neq 0$ has total degree at most $md$, by the Schwartz-Zippel lemma the probability that $g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt)$ is zero over a uniformly random choice of $u_\zpt$ is at most $md/q$. Conditioned on $g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt) \neq 0$, the product $(r_\xpt r_\zpt) \cdot g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt)$ is a uniformly random element of $\F_q$ when $r_\zpt$ is chosen uniformly at random. 
    89		
    90		The probability that $u_\xpt \neq 0, r_\xpt \neq 0, g_{\ind_m(u_\xpt)}(u_\zpt) \neq 0$ is at least $(1 - q^{-m}) \cdot (1 - q^{-1}) \cdot (1 - md/q)$ since $u_\xpt, r_\xpt, u_\zpt$ are chosen independently.
    91		
    92		Since $q = 2^t$ is an admissible field size, we have that for all $a \in \F_q$, the trace of $a$ is equal to $\sum_i a_i$ where $(a_1,\ldots,a_t)=\kappa(a) \in \F_2^t$ are defined in Section~\ref{sec:subfields}. Thus the probability that a uniformly random element of $\F_q$ has trace $0$ is exactly $1/2$. 
    93	\end{proof}

    95	In this appendix we often use the ``$\approx_\delta$'' notation to specify closeness of general operators (not necessarily POVMs) that are indexed by questions but not answers: given sets of operators $\{A^x \}$ and $\{B^x\}$ indexed by questions $x \in \cal{X}$, we write $A^x \approx_\delta B^x$ to denote \[
    96		\E_{x \sim \mu} \bra{\psi} (A^x - B^x)^\dagger (A^x - B^x)
    97	        \ket{\psi}\,\leq\, O(\delta)
    98	      \]
    99	where $\mu$ is a question distribution and $\ket{\psi}$ is a state that has been fixed by context. This will be useful for expressing closeness of observables, for example. The following two lemmas relate the closeness between sets of operators and weighted sums of those operators. 
   100	\begin{lemma}
   101	\label{lem:avg-closeness}
   102	Let $\{A^x \}$ and $\{B^x\}$ be operators indexed by some finite set $\mathcal{X}$, and let $\mu$ be a probability distribution over $\mathcal{X}$. Let $\{\alpha_x \}$ be a set of complex numbers such that $|\alpha_x| \leq 1$. Then if $A^x \approx_\delta B^x$ on average over $x$ drawn from $\mu$, then $A \approx_\delta B$, where $A = \E_x \alpha_x A^x$ and $B= \E_x \alpha_x B^x$.
   103	\end{lemma}
   104	\begin{proof}
   105	Expand
   106	\begin{align*}
   107		\Big\| \E_x \alpha_x \big ( A^x - B^x \big) \ket{\psi} \Big\|^2 &\leq \Big( \E_x \norm{ (A^x -B^x) \ket{\psi}} \Big)^2 \\
   108		&\leq \E_x \norm{(A^x - B^x) \ket{\psi}}^2 \\
   109		&\leq \delta\;.
   110	\end{align*}
   111	The first inequality is the triangle inequality and the second inequality is Jensen's inequality. 
   112	\end{proof}
   113	
   114	\begin{lemma}
   115	\label{lem:povm-to-obs}
   116	Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a finite set. Let $\{A^x_a \}_{a \in \mathcal{A}}$ and $\{B^x_a\}_{a \in \mathcal{A}}$ be POVMs and let $\{ \alpha_a \}_{a \in \mathcal{A}}$ be a collection of complex numbers on the unit circle. Let $A^x = \sum_a \alpha_a A^x_a$ and $B^x = \sum_a  \alpha_a B^x_a$. Then 
   117	\[
   118		A^x_a \approx_\delta B^x_a \quad \text{implies} \quad A^x \approx_{\delta'} B^x
   119	\]
   120	for $\delta' = |\mathcal{A}| \cdot \delta$.
   121	\end{lemma}
   122	\begin{proof}
   123	Expand
   124		\begin{align*}
   125			\E_x \norm{(A^x - B^x) \ket{\psi}}^2 &= \E_x \Big\|\sum_a \alpha_a (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi}\Big\|^2 \\
   126			&\leq \E_x \Big( \sum_a \norm{ (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi}} \Big)^2 \\
   127			&\leq \E_x |\mathcal{A}| \cdot \sum_a \norm{ (A^x_a - B^x_a) \ket{\psi}}^2 \\
   128			&\leq |\mathcal{A}| \cdot \delta\;.
   129		\end{align*}
   130	The first inequality follows from the triangle inequality, the second inequality follows from Cauchy-Schwarz, and the last inequality follows from the assumption that $A^x_a \approx_\delta B^x_a$.

   405	The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli} is the adaptation, to low individual degree, of the analysis of the quantum low-degree test of Natarajan and Vidick; it is developed in Chapters~\ref{chap:qpbt-observables} and~\ref{chap:qpbt-combining} and concluded in Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction}, where the argument is complete only modulo the unresolved divisibility obligation documented in \cite{gap:qpbt_ld-dimension-divisibility}. It relies on the classical soundness theorem (Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness}) and on the rigidity of the Magic Square game (Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-rigidity}).
   406	
   407	The strategies appearing in Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} and in the conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli} are phrased in terms of qudit Pauli measurements and maximally entangled states of $q$-dimensional qudits. For the intended application it is more convenient to work with qubits: since the field sizes $q$ used here are powers of $2$, the conclusions can be restated in terms of qubit EPR pairs and qubit Pauli measurements.

   653	\subsubsection{Bit string representations}
   654	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   655	
   656	As mentioned at the end of \Cref{sec:tms}, we sometimes treat the
   657	inputs and outputs of Turing machines as representing elements of a finite
   658	field, or a vector space over a finite field.
   659	We discuss some important details about bit representations of finite field
   660	elements and arithmetic over finite fields.
   661	
   662	In the paper we only consider fields $\F_{2^k}$ where $k$ is odd. 
   663	
   664	\begin{definition}\label{def:admissible-size}
   665	  A field size $q$ is called an \emph{admissible} field size if $q=2^k$ for odd
   666	  $k$.
   667	\end{definition}
   668	
   669	Elements of $\F_2$ are naturally represented using bits. 
   670	To represent elements of $\F_{2^k}$ as binary strings we require the
   671	specification of a basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   672	Given a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$, every element $a \in \F_{2^k}$
   673	has a unique expansion $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$ and can be represented as the
   674	$k$-bit string corresponding to $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$.
   675	Note that we omitted the subscript $2$ of $\downsize$ as it maps to the linear
   676	space over the prime subfield $\F_2$.
   677	Thus the \emph{binary representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is defined as the
   678	natural binary representation of $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$ (which in turn is the
   679	\emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}).
   680	Throughout the paper we freely associate between the binary representation of a
   681	field element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ and its $\F_2$-representation,
   682	although---technically speaking---these are distinct objects.
   683	
   684	Given the representations $\downsize(a), \downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$, to
   685	compute the binary representation of $a+b$ it suffices to compute the addition
   686	bit-wise, modulo $2$.
   687	Computing the multiplication of elements $a, b$ requires the specification of
   688	the multiplication tables $\{K_{e_i} \in \Matrix_k (\F_2)\}_{i=1}^k $ for the
   689	basis $\{e_i\}$.
   690	Given representations $\downsize(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$, $\downsize(b) =
   691	(b_i)_{i=1}^k$ for $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$ respectively, the representation
   692	$\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ is computed as
   693	\begin{equation}
   694	  \label{eq:eq-mult}
   695	  \downsize(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \, \downsize \bigl( e_i b \bigr) =
   696	  \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \bigl( K_{e_i}\, \downsize (b) \bigr)\;.
   697	\end{equation}
   698	Thus, using our representation for field elements, efficiently performing finite
   699	field arithmetic in $\F_{2^k}$ reduces to having access to the multiplication
   700	table of some basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   701	
   702	The following fact provides an efficient deterministic algorithm for computing a
   703	self-dual normal basis for $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the corresponding
   704	multiplication tables for any odd $k$.
   705	
   706	\begin{lemma}
   707	  \label{lem:efficient_basis}
   708	  There exists a deterministic algorithm that given an odd integer $k > 0$,
   709	  outputs a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the
   710	  multiplication tables of the basis in $\poly(k)$ time.
   711	\end{lemma}
   712	
   713	\begin{proof}
   714		The algorithm of Shoup~\cite[Theorem 3.2]{shoup1990new} shows that for prime
   715	  $p$, an irreducible polynomial in $\Fp[X]$ of degree $k$ can be computed in
   716	  time $\poly(p, k)$.
   717	  Then, the algorithm of Lenstra~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{lenstra1991finding} shows
   718	  that given such an irreducible polynomial, the multiplication table of a
   719	  normal basis of $\F_{p^k}$ over $\Fp$ can be computed in $\poly(k,\log p)$
   720	  time.
   721	  Finally, the algorithm of Wang~\cite{wang1989algorithm} shows that for odd $k$
   722	  and a multiplication table $K$ of a normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$, a
   723	  multiplication table $K'$ for a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   724	  $\F_2$ can be computed in $\poly(k)$ time.
   725	  Putting these three algorithms together yields the claimed statement.
   726	\end{proof}
   727	
   728	For $q=2^k$ for $k$ odd (i.e.\ $q$ is an admissible field size) we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q\to 2}$.
   729	
   730	\begin{lemma}
   731	  \label{lem:one}
   732	  Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ be a self-dual normal basis of
   733	  $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   734	  Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and furthermore the representation
   735	  $\downsize(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all ones vector in
   736	  $\F_2^k$.
   737	\end{lemma}
   738	
   739	\begin{proof}
   740	  Since $\{e_i \}$ is a normal basis, $e_i = \alpha^{2^i}$ for some element
   741	  $\alpha \in \F_{2^k}$.
   742	  Furthermore, for every element $b \in \F_{2^k}$, we have that $\tr(b^2) =
   743	  \tr(b)$.
   744	  This is because
   745	  \[
   746	    \tr(b^2) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} b^{2^{i+1}} =
   747	    \sum_{i = 0}^{k-1} b^{2^i} = \tr(b)\;,
   748	  \]
   749	  where we use that $b^{2^k} = b$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   750	  Since $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$, we get that $\tr(e_i) = \tr(e_j)$ for all $i,j$.
   751	  It cannot be the case that $\tr(e_i) = 0$ for all $i$.
   752	  Suppose that this were the case.
   753	  This would imply that $\tr(b) = 0$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   754	  But then for all $j \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$ and for some $b \neq 0$, we would
   755	  also have by item 1 of \Cref{lem:downsize_field} that $b_j = \tr(b e_j) = 0$ where $b = \sum_j b_j e_j$ with $b_j \in
   756	  \F_2$.
   757	  This implies that $b$ is the all zero element of $\F_{2^k}$, which is a
   758	  contradiction.
   759	  Thus $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i=1, 2, \ldots, k$.

   892	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-game} we describe the Pauli basis test as a nonlocal
   893	game $\game^\pauli$ and show that its question distribution is implementable via
   894	a CL distribution, as we did with the classical low-degree test in

   898	
   899	\subsubsection{The game}
   900	\label{sec:qld-game}
   901	
   902	We start by discussing parameter settings.
   903	The game $\game^\pauli$ is parametrized by a tuple
   904	\[\qldparams = (q,m,d)\;,\] where $q,m,d \in \N$ are integers. 
   905	We sometimes write $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
   906	Pauli basis test on the parameters.
   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,
   931	receives outcome $h_X$, and outputs $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$.
   932	For technical reasons that will become clear shortly,
   933	it will be convenient for the prover's measurement to have two outcomes rather than~$q$ outcomes.
   934	To accomplish this, the verifier also provides the prover with an element $r_X \in \F_q$;
   935	given this, the prover should output not $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$ but $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$, which is an element of $\F_2$.
   936	Similarly, on the $Z$ side, suppose the prover is provided $r_Z \in \F_q$,
   937	performs $\{\tau_h^Z\}$ to receive $h_Z$, and outputs $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \in \F_2$.
   938	Together, these two are a pair of two-outcome measurements, one in the~$X$ basis and one in the~$Z$ basis,
   939	and as it turns out, this pair of measurements either commutes with each other or anticommutes with each other
   940	(this is why we modified the measurements to have only two outcomes).
   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}
   946	If $\gamma = 0$, then these two measurements commute, and if $\gamma = 1$, then these two measurements anticommute
   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).
   948	In the $\gamma = 0$ case, the verifier can check whether these two measurements commute by performing the ``commutation check'',
   949	which asks the provers to simultaneously measure both $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$ and $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z)$ and report their values.
   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.
   957	
   958	\begin{definition}[Admissible parameters]\label{def:admissible}
   959	  We say that the tuple $\qldparams=(q, m, d)$ is \emph{admissible} if $q$ is
   960	  an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $m | q$.
   961	\end{definition}

   965	We now describe the question distribution of the game $\game^\pauli$, and show

   178	Let $p$ be a prime and $q = p^k$ a prime power. We write $\F_p$ and $\F_q$ for
   179	the finite fields with $p$ and $q$ elements; $p$ is the characteristic of
   180	$\F_q$, and $\F_p$ is its prime subfield.
   181	
   182	\begin{definition}[Coordinate map and multiplication tables]\label{def:subfields-kappa}
   183		% The source lets k range over all integers; the extension field exists
   184		% only for k >= 1, so that domain condition is made explicit here.
   185		Let $q$ be a prime power and $k \ge 1$ an integer, so that $\F_q$ is a
   186		subfield of $\F_{q^k}$ and $\F_{q^k}$ is a linear space of dimension $k$
   187		over $\F_q$.
   188		Fix a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The bijection
   189		$\kappa_q : \F_{q^k} \to \F_q^k$ associated with this basis is
   190		\[
   191			\kappa_q : a \mapsto (a_i)_{i=1}^k\;, \qquad
   192			\text{where } a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i\;.
   193		\]
   194		The map $\kappa_q$ is an isomorphism of $\F_q$-vector spaces; in particular
   195		$\kappa_q(a + b) = \kappa_q(a) + \kappa_q(b)$ for all $a, b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   196		Moreover, multiplication by a fixed element corresponds to a linear map:
   197		for every $a \in \F_{q^k}$ there is a matrix $K_a \in \Mat_k(\F_q)$, the
   198		\emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to $\{e_i\}$}, such that
   199		$\kappa_q(ab) = K_a\, \kappa_q(b)$ for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   200		The map extends coordinatewise to vectors, matrices, and sets: for
   201		$v = (v_1, \dots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$ set
   202		$\kappa_q(v) = (\kappa_q(v_i))_{i=1}^n \in \F_q^{kn}$; for
   203		$M = (M_{i,j}) \in \Mat_{m,n}(\F_{q^k})$ let
   204		$\chi_q(M) \in \Mat_{mk,nk}(\F_q)$ be the block matrix whose $(i,j)$-th
   205		block is $K_{M_{i,j}}$; and for a set $S$ of vectors put
   206		$\kappa_q(S) = \{\kappa_q(v) : v \in S\}$. When $q = p$ is the field
   207		characteristic, the subscript is omitted and we write $\kappa$ and $\chi$.
   208	\end{definition}
   209	
   210	\begin{definition}[Admissible field size]\label{def:admissible-size}
   211		A field size $q$ is \emph{admissible} if $q = 2^k$ for an odd integer $k$.
   212	\end{definition}
   213	
   214	Only fields $\F_{2^k}$ with $k$ odd are used in the analysis of the Pauli basis
   215	test.
   216	
   217	\begin{definition}[Trace of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$]\label{def:subfield-trace}
   218		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:admissible-size}
   219		The \emph{trace of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$} is the map
   220		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   221		\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   222			\tr_{q^k \to q} : a \mapsto \Tr(K_a)
   223		\end{equation}
   224		for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $K_a$ is the multiplication table of $a$ with
   225		respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$. The trace is an $\F_q$-linear map from
   226		$\F_{q^k}$ to $\F_q$, and it is independent of the choice of basis, as can
   227		be seen from the equivalent formula
   228		\[
   229			\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   230		\]
   231		For admissible $q = 2^k$ we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q \to 2}$.
   232	\end{definition}
   233	
   234	\begin{definition}[Dual, self-dual, and normal bases]\label{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   235		\uses{def:subfield-trace}
   236		A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', \dots, e_k'\}$ of a basis
   237		$\{e_1, \dots, e_k\}$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$ is a basis such that
   238		$\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for all
   239		$i, j \in \{1, \dots, k\}$. A \emph{self-dual basis} is one equal to its own
   240		dual. If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set
   286		Normality gives $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$ (indices taken cyclically), and
   287		$\tr(b^2) = \tr(b)$ for every $b \in \F_{2^k}$ because squaring permutes the
   288		terms of $\tr(b) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} b^{2^j}$, using $b^{2^k} = b$. Hence all
   289		the values $\tr(e_i)$ coincide. If the common value were $0$, then $\tr$
   290		would vanish identically on $\F_{2^k}$ by linearity; but then item 1 of
   291		Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} would give $\kappa(b) =
   292		(\tr(b e_1), \dots, \tr(b e_k)) = 0$ for every $b$, contradicting the
   293		bijectivity of $\kappa$. Thus $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and item 1 of
   294		Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} gives
   295		$\kappa(1) = (\tr(e_1), \dots, \tr(e_k)) = (1, \dots, 1)$.
   296	\end{proof}
   297	
   298	\begin{definition}[Binary representation of field elements]\label{def:binary-representation}
   299		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:admissible-size,
   300			def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   301		Let $q = 2^k$ be an admissible field size. For each odd $k$ we fix, once and
   302		for all, a self-dual normal basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   303		$\F_2$ together with its multiplication tables
   304		$\{K_{e_i}\}_{i=1}^k$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis});
   305		the maps $\kappa$ and $\tr$ always refer to this basis. The \emph{binary
   306		representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is the $k$-bit string
   307		$\kappa(a) \in \F_2^k$, the \emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}; the two are
   308		freely identified. Addition of representations is bitwise addition modulo
   309		$2$, and multiplication is determined by the multiplication tables through
   310		\begin{equation}\label{eq:eq-mult}
   311			\kappa(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i\, \kappa(e_i b)
   312			= \sum_{i=1}^k a_i \bigl(K_{e_i}\, \kappa(b)\bigr)\;,
   313		\end{equation}
   314		where $\kappa(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$.
   315	\end{definition}

   288	/-- The ordered-edge subtype used by the Pauli question sampler.  This is

   306	/-- The finite support obtained by sampling an edge and a common ambient seed,

   340	inductive PauliAnswer (P : AdmissibleParams) where

   344	  | pairBits (a : ZMod 2 × ZMod 2)

   350	/-- A finite sum code used only to construct the `Fintype` instance for the

   355	abbrev PauliAnswerCode (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
   356	  PauliScalar P ⊕

   358	      ((Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P) ⊕
   359	        ((ZMod 2 × ZMod 2) ⊕
   360	          (ZMod 2 ⊕ ((Fin 3 → ZMod 2) ⊕ PauliRegister P)))))

   362	/-- The constructor-preserving finite-code equivalence for `PauliAnswer`.
   363	Lean-only infrastructure for `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
   364	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   365	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1012-1039`.

   367	noncomputable def pauliAnswerEquiv (P : AdmissibleParams) :
   368	    PauliAnswer P ≃ PauliAnswerCode P where
   369	  toFun
   370	    | .value a => .inl a
   371	    | .alinePoly a => .inr (.inl a)
   372	    | .dlinePoly a => .inr (.inr (.inl a))
   373	    | .pairBits a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a)))
   374	    | .bit a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a))))
   375	    | .msTriple a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a)))))
   376	    | .pauliOutcome a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr a)))))
   377	  invFun
   378	    | .inl a => .value a
   379	    | .inr (.inl a) => .alinePoly a
   380	    | .inr (.inr (.inl a)) => .dlinePoly a
   381	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a))) => .pairBits a
   382	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a)))) => .bit a
   383	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a))))) => .msTriple a
   384	    | .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inr a))))) => .pauliOutcome a
   385	  left_inv := by
   386	    intro x
   387	    cases x <;> rfl
   388	  right_inv := by
   389	    intro x
   390	    cases x with
   391	    | inl a => rfl
   392	    | inr x =>
   393	        cases x with
   394	        | inl a => rfl
   395	        | inr x =>
   396	            cases x with
   397	            | inl a => rfl
   398	            | inr x =>
   399	                cases x with
   400	                | inl a => rfl
   401	                | inr x =>
   402	                    cases x with
   403	                    | inl a => rfl
   404	                    | inr x =>
   405	                        cases x with
   406	                        | inl a => rfl
   407	                        | inr a => rfl

   415	/-- The phase bit `γ(u_X,u_Z,r_X,r_Z)` from `eq:gamma-value`.  It uses the
   416	fixed trace selected by `P.model`, as required by the paper's fixed
   417	self-dual-normal representation.  Blueprint
   418	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`; paper origin
   419	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1198-1212`.
   420	-/
   421	noncomputable def gammaValue (P : AdmissibleParams)
   422	    (uX uZ : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P)
   423	    (rX rZ : PauliScalar P) : ZMod 2 :=
   424	  fixedBinTrace P.model
   425	    (dotProduct (rX • indicatorVec uX) (rZ • indicatorVec uZ))
   426	
   427	/-- The commutation bit attached to a full Pauli ambient question, from
   428	`eq:gamma-value` in `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
   429	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   430	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1198-1212`.
   431	-/
   432	noncomputable def pauliPairGamma (P : AdmissibleParams) (z : PauliSpace P) : ZMod 2 :=
   433	  gammaValue P (pauliXBlock z) (pauliZBlock z)
   434	    (pauliRXBlock z) (pauliRZBlock z)
   435	
   436	/-- The answer constructor prescribed by each Pauli question type; this is the
   437	well-formedness part of `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
   438	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   439	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1012-1039`.
   440	-/
   441	def validPauliAnswer (t : PauliType) (a : PauliAnswer P) : Bool :=
   442	  match t, a with
   443	  | .point _, .value _ => true
   444	  | .aline _, .alinePoly _ => true
   445	  | .dline _, .dlinePoly _ => true
   446	  | .pauli _, .pauliOutcome _ => true
   447	  | .pairW _, .bit _ => true
   448	  | .pair, .pairBits _ => true
   449	  | .ms (.constraint _), .msTriple _ => true
   450	  | .ms (.var _), .bit _ => true
   451	  | _, _ => false
   452	
   453	/-- The axis-line versus point relation used by `def:pauli-win-predicate`,
   454	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   455	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1012-1039`.
   456	-/
   457	def pauliAlinePointCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   458	    (line point : PauliSpace P) (f : Fin (P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P)
   459	    (a : PauliScalar P) : Prop :=
   460	  -- The universal form preserves the source's zero-direction convention.
   461	  ∀ t : PauliScalar P,
   462	    pauliPointBlock W point =
   463	        pauliPointBlock W line + t • coordinateDirection
   464	          (chiIndex P.toLdParams (pauliScalarBlock line)) →
   465	      evalCoefficient f t = a
   466	
   467	/-- The diagonal-line versus point relation used by `def:pauli-win-predicate`,
   468	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   469	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1012-1039`.
   470	-/
   471	def pauliDlinePointCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   472	    (line point : PauliSpace P) (f : Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P)
   473	    (a : PauliScalar P) : Prop :=
   474	  ∀ t : PauliScalar P,
   475	    pauliPointBlock W point = pauliPointBlock W line +
   476	        t • pauliDirectionBlock line →
   477	      evalCoefficient f t = a
   478	
   479	/-- The raw Pauli-versus-point consistency relation from `def:pauli-win-predicate`,
   480	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   481	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1012-1039`.
   482	-/
   483	def pauliPointPauliCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   484	    (point : PauliSpace P) (h : PauliRegister P) (a : PauliScalar P) : Prop :=
   485	  lowDegreeEnc h (pauliPointBlock W point) = a
   486	
   487	/-- The Pair/W consistency relation, including the one-sided gamma gate, from
   488	`def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   489	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1012-1039`.
   490	-/
   491	def pauliPairCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   492	    (z : PauliSpace P) (β : ZMod 2) (bits : ZMod 2 × ZMod 2) : Prop :=
   493	  pauliPairGamma P z ≠ 0 ∨
   494	    (match W with
   495	    | .X => bits.1 = β
   496	    | .Z => bits.2 = β)
   497	
   498	/-- The point/Pair/W trace consistency relation from `def:pauli-win-predicate`,
   499	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   500	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1012-1039`.
   501	-/
   502	def pauliPointPairCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   503	    (z : PauliSpace P) (a : PauliScalar P) (β : ZMod 2) : Prop :=
   504	  pauliPairGamma P z ≠ 0 ∨
   505	    fixedBinTrace P.model
   506	      (a * (match W with
   507	      | .X => pauliRXBlock z
   508	      | .Z => pauliRZBlock z)) = β
   509	
   510	/-- The Point/Variable consistency clause of `def:pauli-win-predicate`.
   511	The check is gated by `gamma = 0` and only uses Variable 1 in the X basis or
   512	Variable 5 in the Z basis.  Blueprint
   513	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`; paper origin
   514	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1012-1039`.
   515	-/
   516	def pauliPointVariableCondition (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   517	    (z : PauliSpace P) (j : Fin 9) (a : PauliScalar P) (β : ZMod 2) : Prop :=
   518	  pauliPairGamma P z = 0 ∨
   519	    (j = ⟨0, by decide⟩ ∧ W = .X ∧
   520	        fixedBinTrace P.model (a * pauliRXBlock z) = β) ∨
   521	    (j = ⟨4, by decide⟩ ∧ W = .Z ∧
   522	        fixedBinTrace P.model (a * pauliRZBlock z) = β)
   523	
   524	/-- The Pauli win predicate, with constructor-shape rejection.  This is
   525	`def:pauli-win-predicate` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`,
   526	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1012-1039`.
   527	-/
   528	noncomputable def pauliWinPredicate (P : AdmissibleParams) :
   529	    PauliQuestion P → PauliQuestion P → PauliAnswer P → PauliAnswer P → Bool :=
   530	  open Classical in
   531	  fun (tA, xA) (tB, xB) a b =>
   532	    if validPauliAnswer tA a && validPauliAnswer tB b then
   533	      match tA, tB, a, b with
   534	      | .point W, .point W', .value u, .value v =>
   535	          decide (W = W' ∧ u = v)
   536	      | .aline W, .point W', .alinePoly f, .value u =>
   537	          decide (W = W' ∧ pauliAlinePointCondition P W xA xB f u)
   538	      | .point W, .aline W', .value u, .alinePoly f =>
   539	          decide (W = W' ∧ pauliAlinePointCondition P W xB xA f u)
   540	      | .dline W, .point W', .dlinePoly f, .value u =>
   541	          decide (W = W' ∧ pauliDlinePointCondition P W xA xB f u)
   542	      | .point W, .dline W', .value u, .dlinePoly f =>
   543	          decide (W = W' ∧ pauliDlinePointCondition P W xB xA f u)
   544	      | .point W, .pauli W', .value u, .pauliOutcome h =>
   545	          decide (W = W' ∧ pauliPointPauliCondition P W xA h u)
   546	      | .pauli W, .point W', .pauliOutcome h, .value u =>
   547	          decide (W = W' ∧ pauliPointPauliCondition P W xB h u)
   548	      | .pairW W, .pair, .bit β, .pairBits bits =>
   549	          decide (pauliPairCondition P W xA β bits)
   550	      | .pair, .pairW W, .pairBits bits, .bit β =>
   551	          decide (pauliPairCondition P W xB β bits)
   552	      | .point W, .pairW W', .value u, .bit β =>
   553	          decide (W = W' ∧ pauliPointPairCondition P W xA u β)
   554	      | .pairW W, .point W', .bit β, .value u =>
   555	          decide (W = W' ∧ pauliPointPairCondition P W xB u β)
   556	      | .ms t, .ms t', .msTriple u, .msTriple v =>
   557	          decide (pauliPairGamma P xA = 0 ∨
   558	            msWinPredicate t t' (.triple u) (.triple v))
   559	      | .ms t, .ms t', .bit u, .bit v =>
   560	          decide (pauliPairGamma P xA = 0 ∨
   561	            msWinPredicate t t' (.bit u) (.bit v))
   562	      | .point W, .ms (.var j), .value u, .bit β =>
   563	          decide (pauliPointVariableCondition P W xB j u β)
   564	      | .ms (.var j), .point W, .bit β, .value u =>
   565	          decide (pauliPointVariableCondition P W xA j u β)
   566	      | .aline W, .aline W', .alinePoly f, .alinePoly g => decide (W = W' ∧ f = g)
   567	      | .dline W, .dline W', .dlinePoly f, .dlinePoly g => decide (W = W' ∧ f = g)
   568	      | .pauli W, .pauli W', .pauliOutcome u, .pauliOutcome v =>
   569	          decide (W = W' ∧ u = v)
   570	      | .pairW W, .pairW W', .bit u, .bit v => decide (W = W' ∧ u = v)
   571	      | .pair, .pair, .pairBits u, .pairBits v => decide (u = v)
   572	      | _, _, _, _ => true
   573	    else false
   574	
   575	/-- The Pauli basis test game.  This is `def:pauli-question-distribution` and
   576	`def:pauli-win-predicate` packaged as the symmetric game of
   577	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-367`, paper origin
   578	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:979-1039`.
   579	-/
   580	noncomputable def pauliBasisTest (P : AdmissibleParams) : Game where
   581	  QuestionA := PauliQuestion P
   582	  QuestionB := PauliQuestion P
   583	  AnswerA := PauliAnswer P
   584	  AnswerB := PauliAnswer P
   585	  μ := pauliQuestionDistribution P
   586	  μ_prob := by sorry
   587	  decide := pauliWinPredicate P
   588

950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).

   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.

   958	\begin{definition}[Admissible parameters]\label{def:admissible}
   959	  We say that the tuple $\qldparams=(q, m, d)$ is \emph{admissible} if $q$ is
   960	  an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $m | q$.
   961	\end{definition}

   963	
   964	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   965	We now describe the question distribution of the game $\game^\pauli$, and show
   966	that it is a (typed) CL distribution.
   967	The question types in the game $\game^\pauli$ are
   968	\begin{equation}
   969	  \label{eq:pauli-type}
   970	  \type^\pauli= \bigl( \{\Point, \ALine, \DLine, \Pauli, \Pair \} \times \{X,Z\} \bigr)
   971	  \cup \type^\ms \cup \{\Pair\}\;,
   972	\end{equation}
   973	where $\type^\ms$ is the question type set of the Magic Square game defined in
   974	Section~\ref{sec:ms}.
   975	
   976	
   977	
   978	
   979	Before presenting the CL functions of the Pauli basis test, we first give an
   980	intuitive description of the question distribution of the Pauli basis test: a
   981	pair of questions $((\tvar_\alice, x_\alice), (\tvar_\bob, x_\bob))$ in
   982	$\game^\pauli$ can be sampled via the following procedure:
   983	
   984	\begin{enumerate}
   985	\item Sample a pair of types by sampling an edge $(\tvar_\alice, \tvar_\bob)$ of
   986	  the graph $G^\pauli$ given in Figure~\ref{fig:type-graph-pauli} uniformly at
   987	  random (including the self-loops).
   988	\item Sample the following uniformly at random:
   989		\begin{enumerate}
   990		\item (\emph{Points}) $u_\xpt,u_\zpt \in \F_q^m$,
   991		\item (\emph{Directions}) $s \in \F_q$, $v \in \F_q^m$,
   992	  \item (\emph{Qubit basis for (anti-)commutation}) $r_\xpt,r_\zpt \in \F_q$.
   993		\end{enumerate}
   994	\item For $w \in \AB$ and $W\in\{X,Z\}$,
   995		\begin{enumerate}
   996	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Point, W)$, then set $x_w = u_W$,
   997	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\ALine, W)$, then set $x_w = (u_0,s)$, where $u_0 =
   998	    L^\lnf_{e_i}(u_W)$, with $i = \chi(s)$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-game} for
   999	    definition of $L^\lnf$ and $\chi(s)$),
  1000	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\DLine,W)$, then set $x_w = (u_0,s,v')$, where $i =
  1001	    \chi(s)$, $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v)$, and $u_0 = L^\lnf_{v'}(u_W)$,
  1002	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Constraint_i$ for some $i\in\{1,\ldots,6\}$, then set
  1003	    $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1004	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Variable_j$ for some $j\in\{1,\ldots,9\}$, then set $x_w
  1005	    = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1006	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Pair$, then set $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1007	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Pair, W)$, then set $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1008	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Pauli, W)$, then set $x_w = 0$.
  1009		\end{enumerate}
  1010	\end{enumerate}
